activities.title: Practical Context: The Clear Glass Viewing Window

analogy.headline: Practical Context: The Clear Glass Viewing Window
analogy.story:
Imagine a reinforced museum display case containing an unidentified artifact behind thick glass: DisplayCase<?>. As a museum visitor looking through the glass, you can safely inspect the object and confirm it is a physical entity (read it as an Object).

However, the display case has a sealed slot: you are strictly forbidden from shoving random items through the slot (you cannot put a coffee cup or textbook inside) because you do not know the exact environmental classification of what is already inside. The only thing that can pass through the slot is literally empty space (null).

This is the exact contract of the unbounded wildcard: safe for universal inspection, locked against blind mutation.
analogy.keyTakeaway: List<?> represents a list of some unknown type: you can safely read elements as Object, but you cannot write any object into it because its concrete type is unknown.

activities.title: Generics Invariance & The Unbounded Wildcard (?) Contract

keyTakeaways: Generics are strictly invariant: List<String> does NOT inherit from List<Object>
Java arrays are covariant (String[] is an Object[]), which causes runtime ArrayStoreException crashes
The wildcard (?) denotes an unknown type; List<?> is the supertype of all List<T> instantiations
You can safely read from List<?> (yields Object), but you CANNOT add any object to it (except literal null)

activities.content:
### Why Generics Are Invariant

In Java, `String` is a subtype of `Object`. Naturally, many developers assume that `List<String>` must be a subtype of `List<Object>`. **It is not!** Generics are strictly **invariant**.

**Proof of Why Invariance Is Necessary:**
Suppose `List<String>` were a subtype of `List<Object>`:
```java
List<String> stringList = new ArrayList<>();
List<Object> objectList = stringList; // If Java allowed this...

// A valid operation on List<Object>:
objectList.add(Integer.valueOf(42));

// Now stringList contains an Integer! When we read:
String str = stringList.get(0); // FATAL RUNTIME ClassCastException!
```
To preserve compile-time type safety and guarantee that collections cannot be corrupted through aliases, Java makes parameterized types invariant.

---

### Contrast: Java Array Covariance Flaw

Unlike Generics, Java arrays are **covariant**: `String[]` is treated as a subtype of `Object[]`. This historical design causes severe runtime defects:
```java
String[] strArray = new String[2];
Object[] objArray = strArray; // Allowed by Java array covariance!
objArray[0] = Integer.valueOf(99); // Compiles! Crashes at runtime with ArrayStoreException!
```
Generics were intentionally designed to be invariant specifically to prevent this runtime flaw.

---

### The Solution: The Unbounded Wildcard (`?`)

If you want a method to process a list of *any* type without caring what that type is, use the unbounded wildcard `List<?>`:
```java
public static void printList(List<?> list) {
    for (Object elem : list) {
        System.out.println(elem);
    }
}
```
`List<?>` is the universal supertype of all parameterized lists (`List<String>`, `List<Integer>`, `List<Double>`).

---

### The Immutable Writing Restriction on `List<?>`

Because the concrete element type of `List<?>` is unknown to the compiler:
```java
List<?> unknownList = new ArrayList<String>();
// unknownList.add("hello"); // COMPILE ERROR: The method add(capture#1-of ?) is not applicable
// unknownList.add(new Object()); // COMPILE ERROR!
unknownList.add(null); // The ONLY value permitted, because null belongs to all reference types
```
You can read elements (which are safely typed as `Object`), inspect `list.size()`, and clear the list, but you cannot insert objects.

---

### Executable Demonstration: Invariance vs Unbounded Wildcard

questions.question: Why does the statement 'List<Object> list = new ArrayList<String>();' fail to compile?
options: Because ArrayList does not implement List
Because Generics are invariant: List<String> is not a subtype of List<Object>
Because String does not extend Object
Because new ArrayList requires diamond brackets in Java
questions.explanation: Generics are invariant. If List<String> were assignable to List<Object>, non-string objects could be added through the List<Object> reference, corrupting the type safety of the underlying string list.

questions.question: What is the only element value that can be added to a List<?> via its add() method?
options: Nothing at all, not even null
questions.explanation: Because the exact type of List<?> is unknown, the compiler cannot verify if any concrete object is compatible. The only exception is null, which is a valid value for all reference types in Java.

activities.title: Senior Engineer Interview: List<?> vs List<Object>

qaList.question: What is the precise difference between 'List<Object>' and 'List<?>', and when should each be used?
qaList.answer:
'List<Object>' means a list parameterized specifically by java.lang.Object. Because generics are invariant, you can ONLY pass a List<Object> to a method expecting List<Object> (you cannot pass List<String> or List<Integer>). You can add any Object into a List<Object>.

Conversely, 'List<?>' means a list of some UNKNOWN type. You can pass ANY list (List<String>, List<Integer>, List<Double>) to a method expecting List<?>. However, you cannot add any object into a List<?> (except null) because the compiler cannot determine the actual underlying type.

Use List<Object> when building a heterogeneous collection that explicitly accepts any object. Use List<?> when building read-only utility methods that inspect arbitrary lists.

practiceProblems.title: Universal Collection Emptiness & Size Reporter
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a static method reportStatus(List<?> list) that returns a string formatted as 'Empty' if the list is null or empty, or 'Size: N' where N is the size of the list.

practiceProblems.title: Verify Identical Dimensions of Disparate Lists
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method haveEqualSize(List<?> listA, List<?> listB) that returns true if both non-null lists have the same number of elements.

practiceProblems.title: Wildcard Null Presence Verification
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method containsAnyNull(List<?> list) that returns true if any element in the list is null, using the unbounded wildcard.

practiceProblems.title: Convert Arbitrary Generic List to String List
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method convertToStrings(List<?> list) that accepts a list of any type and returns a new List<String> where each element is converted via String.valueOf().

practiceProblems.title: Audit Shared Element Count Across Unknown Lists
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method countSharedElements(List<?> listA, List<?> listB) that returns how many elements in listA also appear in listB (using Objects.equals()).
